## What it is

- From **Trinidad and Tobago**, developed in the 1930s-40s out of Carnival percussion (tamboo bamboo); made from 55-gallon oil drums from about 1947; the national instrument (Wikipedia, "Steelpan").
- The tenor (lead) pan's notes are laid out in **fourths and fifths**, Anthony Williams's arrangement, now the standard for lead pans (Wikipedia). The ring order and range drawn here (a low-C tenor, 29 notes) are unverified: makers differ.
- These are living traditions with their own teachers, names and ways of playing. The site's sound is a sketch from a few physics ideas, not the instrument; anything not from a source named on this page is marked unverified.

## How it sounds

- Each note is a shaped area of the steel; the **bigger** the area, the **lower** the note (Wikipedia).
- Tuners tune not only the note but its **overtones**: fundamental, second and third partial (Wikipedia: Bertie Marshall and Alan Gervais). Here those are at **1 : 2 : 3** (the note, its octave, the octave and a fifth).
- A stroke near the edge of the area brings out the upper partials; a harder stick tip is brighter (the site's amounts).

## Works Cited

::: {.works-cited}
"Steelpan." *Wikipedia*, Wikimedia Foundation, [en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steelpan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steelpan). Trinidad and Tobago, 1930s-40s, from tamboo bamboo; national instrument; 55-gallon drums from about 1947; TASPO 1951; Anthony Williams's fourths and fifths layout, standard for lead pans; overtone tuning (fundamental, second, third partial) by Bertie Marshall and Alan Gervais; bigger area lower; tuned with hammers and strobe tuners.

**For students**

"Ellie Mannette." *Wikipedia*, Wikimedia Foundation, [en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellie_Mannette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellie_Mannette). Trinidadian pan maker and player, "father of the modern steel drum"; sank the drum's top; 1999 National Heritage Fellowship.
:::
